newsitem.title: USA: AT&T results skid; in line with lowered expectations.
newsitem.headline: AT&T results skid; in line with lowered expectations.

text.p: AT&T Corp., which last week shocked Wall Street by announcing that its chairman-in-waiting had resigned under pressure, Monday reported a 36 percent decline in profits for the latest quarter.
It said it earned $959 million in its second quarter, down from $1.5 billion a year earlier, as investments in new markets trimmed results.
The company said it earned 59 cents a share on revenue of $13.2 billion. A year earlier, AT&T earned 92 cents a share on sales of $12.9 billion.

The income was in line with Wall Street's expectations that the company would earn 58 cents a share, according to estimates compiled by First Call. AT&T's shares were unchanged at $34.375 in early trading on the New York Stock Exchange.

"While we are making good progress against the commitments we made to our investors earlier this year, we're certainly not pleased with the year-over-year decline in our earnings," said AT&T Chairman Robert Allen. "Our results reflect the short-term effect of our strategy to strengthen and grow the business over the long term."

The telecommunications giant shocked the industry and Wall Street last Wednesday when John Walter, who had been handpicked last November to succeed Allen, suddenly resigned. The company's board said it would not promote him to chief executive next January, as originally planned, because it had decided he was not suited to the job.
AT&T said income in the second quarter was reduced by its investments in wireless and local phone service and the Internet.
Its revenue increase was driven by growth in business long-distance services, wireless services and AT&T Solutions, its systems integration business. Financial services revenue declined.

Core long-distance revenue for the quarter increased 1.5 percent to $11.58 billion. Long-distance call volumes grew 9.7 percent from the 1996 second quarter and declined 0.5 percent over the first quarter of 1997.
Revenue growth lagged the 8 percent growth seen at rival Sprint Corp., and the 4 percent to 5 percent growth expected from MCI Communications Corp.
That translates into further market share losses for the struggling telephone giant, which serves about 80 million residential customers and 10 million business customers.
Analysts said there were few surprises in the second-quarter report that would lead them to sustantially revise their opinions of the prospects for AT&T's lagging stock.
"They came in slightly ahead of anticipated," CS First Boston analyst Frank Governali said. "But there is nothing here that should cause a major change in the view of their prospects."

AT&T Chief Financial Officer Dan Somers said the decline in its second-quarter earnings would be the low point for the company, and year-over-year earnings comparisons should become more favourable in future quarters.

The increased revenue-to-volume gap resulted from the continued effects of pricing pressures on new business contracts, changes in product mix, the use of free calling minutes as a customer retention tool and the increased customer acceptance of calling plans, the company said.
Revenue from communications services rose 3 percent from a year ago to $12.8 billion in the second quarter.
Wireless revenue rose 14 percent to $1.09 billion.
Financial services revenue declined to $351 million, a decline of 16.3 percent, primarily reflecting the impact of a securitization programme at AT&T Universal Card Services.

Allen said the company remains committed to delivering on its overall financial targets, "despite the fact that our local service efforts have been slowed by the foot-dragging of entrenched monopolies."
Business long-distance revenue rose $223 million to $5.6 billion in the quarter, up 4.1 percent from a year ago, driven by strong double-digit growth in data services.

Business volume growth, led by toll-free services, was in the mid-teens. The volume increase was almost entirely offset by the continued impact of lower prices in new contracts with business customers and a change in product mix.
Revenue from consumer long-distance services declined $50 million to $6.0 billion in the quarter, down less than 1 percent, with volume growth slightly below the industry rate.

New retention and acquisition programmes that provide free minutes to customers reduced the revenue growth rate by about 1.6 percent. As a result of aggressive promotional pricing, international volumes had double-digit growth, while revenue declined slightly.
At the end of the quarter, AT&T had 7.6 million cellular telephone subscribers, up 23.3 percent from a year earlier.
The AT&T Worldnet Internet access service ended the quarter with a subscriber base of about 923,000.
